title: Recover Binary Search Tree
statement:
You get `root`, the root of a binary tree that used to be a valid binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree were smaller than the node's value and all values in its right subtree were larger. Then the values held by exactly two of its nodes were exchanged by mistake.

Repair the tree in place by putting those two values back, without adding, removing or relinking any node. The function returns nothing; the tree itself is checked afterwards.
constraints: Exchanging the values of exactly two nodes makes the tree a valid binary search tree
notes:
## Intuition

An in-order walk (left subtree, node, right subtree) of a valid binary search tree visits the values in increasing order. Exchanging two values breaks that order in a predictable way: the larger value now shows up too early and the smaller one too late. So we walk in order, watch for places where a value is smaller than the one before it, and read the two culprits off those places. The brute-force alternative collects all values, sorts them and writes them back in in-order, which costs O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space.

## Approach

1. Keep `prev`, the node visited just before the current one, plus `first` and `second`, the two misplaced nodes.
2. Run `inorder`: visit the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree.
3. At each node, a drop (`prev.val > node.val`) marks a broken spot. On the first drop, `prev` is the too-large value, so store it in `first`. At every drop, store `node` in `second`; the last drop holds the too-small value.
4. Move `prev` to the current node before going right.
5. After the walk, exchange `first.val` and `second.val` using `temp`.

## Example 1, step by step

`root = [1,3,null,null,2]`: node 1 has left child 3, and 3 has right child 2. The in-order walk visits 3, 2, 1. At 3 there is no `prev` yet, so `prev` becomes 3. At 2, `3 > 2` is a drop: `first` = node 3 and `second` = node 2. At 1, `2 > 1` is another drop: `first` stays node 3 and `second` becomes node 1. Exchanging their values gives `[3,1,null,null,2]`, whose in-order walk is 1, 2, 3.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): every node is visited once.
- Space: O(h) for the recursion, where h is the tree height (O(n) for a chain). A Morris traversal, which threads temporary links back to ancestors, brings this down to O(1).

## Pitfalls

- When the two swapped values are next to each other in in-order there is only one drop; setting `second` at every drop covers both cases.
- Take `first` from the earlier node of the first drop (`prev`) and `second` from the later node of the last drop (`node`); swapping the other pair leaves the tree broken.
- Comparing each node only with its parent is not enough: in Example 2, value 2 is a fine left child of 4 but sits in the right subtree of 3.
- Change only values; moving nodes around would alter the structure.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `prev` | node visited just before the current one in in-order |
| `first` | the misplaced node holding the too-large value |
| `second` | the misplaced node holding the too-small value |
| `inorder` | recursive in-order walk |
| `node` | node currently being visited |
| `temp` | holds one value during the exchange |
